reviewNotes: The pitching-kinetics section, its objective and its quiz were removed: the only source (Fleisig 1995) is a primary study, which the claim pipeline does not admit, and no qualifying systematic review states those two moments (the 2023 normative meta-analysis by Mine et al. does not).
The rotation record is qualitative (no angles or totals), because a trainer set-up without a defined zero and stabilisation cannot give repeatable numbers.
The stop blocks use SAFETY.md's tiers: persistent night pain with stiffness is routine; persistent pins and needles is urgent; inability to move after trauma is emergency.
Throwing workload is stated as Spindle policy, not science. The cross-sport paragraph makes no claim about shared mechanics.

claimSlots.statement: Evidence linking shoulder range of motion to injury in overhead athletes is uncertain and sport-specific: no statistically significant pooled association for the measures examined (2018 meta-analysis); external rotation insufficiency associated with injury in professional pitchers from three pooled studies, interpreted with caution (2020 meta-analysis of prospective cohorts); range among several risk factors, with inconsistent injury definitions (2025 systematic review).

scenarios.prompt: A 15-year-old pitcher says the shoulder hurts after games.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Stop throwing and shoulder loading in the session; urgent: tell the athlete and a parent or carer to get an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 the same day for referral to trauma and orthopaedics; emergency if any emergency sign.

lesson.title: Throwing and rotation
lesson.summary: Throwing puts the shoulder through fast, large rotations. Support throwers with strength and sensible workload, record range the same way over time, and know the warning signs.
objectives: Describe the range differences professional pitchers' throwing shoulders typically show.
Explain why the evidence does not establish reliable injury prediction from shoulder range alone.
Know the warning signs in throwers, and refer young throwers with shoulder pain urgently.

blocks.content: This lesson gives a strength coach's view of the throwing shoulder. Throwing workload and return-to-throwing decisions belong to the athlete's sport coach and clinician.

In professional baseball pitchers, the throwing shoulder typically has less internal rotation and more external rotation than the other shoulder. Across the pitchers studied, the twist of the upper arm bone (humeral retroversion) also differed between the two arms, by about 15 degrees on average.
Range and injury risk: still uncertain

Whether shoulder range is linked to injury is uncertain and differs by sport. A 2018 meta-analysis found no statistically significant pooled association between the range measures it examined and shoulder or elbow injury in overhead athletes. A 2020 meta-analysis of prospective studies linked too little extra external rotation in the throwing arm to injury in professional pitchers, from three pooled studies, with a caution about the small number of studies, and suggested range screening may not identify risk in some other overhead sports. A 2025 review listed range among several risk factors and noted that studies define injury differently.
So do not set out to make a thrower's two shoulders match, and do not treat one range record as a verdict. Record rotation on both sides the same way over time.

content.caption: Planned diagram, not available yet: the lying rotation record position.

content: Use one set-up every time: the athlete lies on their back, arm out to the side at shoulder height, elbow bent to a right angle, with a folded towel under the elbow so the upper arm is level.
Ask them to keep the shoulder blade and the back flat on the bench throughout. If either lifts, note it rather than counting that range.
The athlete turns the forearm up toward the head, then down toward the feet, on their own. You do not push.

Write down where the forearm stops in each direction in plain words, compared with the floor: for example "short of level", "level" or "past level". This record is qualitative; it gives no angles or totals.
Record both sides at the same time of day, before training, and look for change across the season. This is a training record, not a test.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: If pain comes on or rises, or any warning sign appears: Stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session. Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling in the arm or shoulder: urgent, today. A new inability to lift or move the arm themselves, without an injury: urgent, today. After a fall or impact, an arm they cannot move or a shoulder that looks out of place: emergency, now. Do not move the arm or try to put it back. Pain and stiffness that do not go away, including pain that is worse at night: routine referral. Pain that is getting worse: routine referral now; do not wait. Anyone under 18 with shoulder pain: urgent, today; tell a parent or carer. This never clears anyone and never names an injury.

blocks.content: Build strength for the rotator cuff and the shoulder blade muscles, rotation strength through the trunk and hips, and controlled deceleration work. Progress one thing at a time, with the same stop rules as lesson 6.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: If pain comes on or rises, or any warning sign appears: Stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session. Pain while throwing, a loss of velocity with pain, or a "dead arm": stop throwing as well as shoulder loading, and refer at the tier that matches. Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling in the arm or shoulder: urgent, today. Pain that is getting worse: routine referral now; do not wait. Anyone under 18 with shoulder pain: urgent, today; tell a parent or carer. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 the same day, for referral to trauma and orthopaedics. This never clears anyone and never names an injury.

content.label: Spindle policy
content.text: Throwing workload, pitch counts and return-to-throwing decisions are for the athlete's sport coach and treating clinician. Your strength work supports that plan; it does not replace it. Your training is not treatment for a diagnosed condition. A client with diagnosed shoulder pain, or one recovering from surgery, a dislocation or a fracture, trains within the treating clinician's plan, and you do not progress that plan on your own. This is Spindle's rule for trainers, not a research finding.

blocks.content: Coaches in other rotational sports, such as racquet sports, swimming and combat sports, can use the same approach: record range the same way over time, build strength, follow the stop rules, and agree workload with the sport coach.

content.prompt: What range pattern does a professional pitcher's throwing shoulder typically show?
options: Less internal rotation and more external rotation than the other side
More internal rotation and less external rotation
content.explanation: The throwing shoulder typically shows less internal and more external rotation; the twist of the upper arm bone also differed between the arms on average.

content.prompt: Can shoulder range alone tell you which overhead athletes will be injured?
options: No: the evidence does not establish reliable prediction from range alone; pooled associations were not significant or were limited to some sports
content.explanation: Syntheses disagree and differ by sport, and injury definitions vary. These findings do not establish reliable prediction of injury from range alone.
